opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting near-term applications of interpretability, honestly. The basic picture is that a lot of what we'd call "personality" in a language model (how sycophantic it is, how confident or hedgy it sounds, whether it's warm or terse, whether it tends toward deception under pressure) seems to be represented in the model's internals in surprisingly structured ways. Often you can find directions in activation space, sometimes people call them persona vectors or steering vectors, that track these traits pretty cleanly.

Once you have that, a few things become possible during training. The first is monitoring. Right now, when you fine-tune a model, say with RLHF or on some new dataset, you mostly find out about personality drift after the fact, by running evals and noticing, oh, the model got a lot more flattering. If you have a reliable internal measure of a trait, you can watch it shift checkpoint by checkpoint, and catch it early, before it shows up clearly in behavior.

The second is data attribution. You can ask which training examples are pushing the model along that sycophancy direction, and filter or reweight them. That's nice because a lot of these shifts come from data that doesn't look obviously problematic to a human reviewer.

The third, which I find most interesting, is intervening on the training process itself. There's this idea that's sort of counterintuitive: you can steer the model *toward* an undesirable trait during fine-tuning, so the gradient doesn't need to build that trait into the weights, and then remove the steering at inference. It's almost like a vaccine. The model doesn't learn the bad disposition because it was already supplied externally.

I'll add a caveat, though, because I think people get overexcited. These linear directions are an approximation. Traits like "honesty" are probably messier and more context-dependent than one vector, and if you optimize hard against a probe, the model can learn to express the behavior in ways your probe doesn't catch. So I see interpretability as a really useful instrument panel and a lever, but you still need behavioral evaluation alongside it. The two together are much stronger than either alone.

r001.rationale: It says personality traits are represented in the model’s internals in structured ways and describes directions in activation space that track them.

r002.rationale: It proposes monitoring traits, tracing their training data, and intervening during fine-tuning to steer personality.

r003.rationale: It describes interpretability as a useful instrument and lever, but does not say it provides stronger guarantees than relying solely on training data; it also notes that probes are approximate and behavioral evaluation remains necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that "personality" in a language model isn't some vague, emergent thing we can only observe from the outside. It's represented somewhere in the network, and interpretability is the set of tools that lets us actually find those representations and, ideally, do something with them.

The simplest version of this is what people have been calling persona vectors or steering vectors. You take a trait you care about, say sycophancy or a tendency toward confident hallucination, and you find a direction in the model's activation space that corresponds to it. You can do that by contrasting activations when the model is behaving that way versus when it isn't. Once you have that direction, you have a lever. You can monitor it during training to see if a fine-tuning run is quietly pushing the model toward a trait you didn't want. That's really valuable, because right now a lot of personality drift gets discovered after the fact, when users notice the model has gotten weirdly flattering or evasive.

The more interesting use is intervening during training rather than just monitoring. There are a couple of ways to do that. One is to add a regularization term that penalizes the model for moving along an undesirable direction, so the optimization is explicitly told "don't become more of this." Another approach, which I find kind of elegant, is almost the opposite: you deliberately steer the model toward the trait during training on the data that would otherwise induce it. The idea is that if the training data has some property that would push the model toward, say, being more deceptive, you supply that shift through the steering vector instead, so the gradient doesn't have to encode it into the weights. It's a bit like a vaccine. You absorb the pressure in a controllable place rather than letting it get baked in.

What I'd caution is that these vectors are approximations. Personality is high-dimensional, and a single linear direction is going to capture the dominant component of a trait, not the whole thing. So you need good behavioral evaluations alongside the mechanistic signal, because the model can shift in ways your vector doesn't see. But the big shift here is that interpretability moves from being a diagnostic you run on a finished model to being a control surface you can use while the model is still being shaped. That's where I think it starts to pay off in a serious way.

r001.rationale: It says personality traits are represented in the network and describes finding trait-related directions in activation space.

r002.rationale: It proposes monitoring trait directions and intervening during training with regularization or steering to control personality traits.

r003.rationale: It describes interpretability as a controllable training lever, but does not clearly claim it provides stronger guarantees about personality than relying solely on training data.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability could help us turn something fairly vague, like a model’s “personality,” into more specific things we can study and influence. Do we mean how agreeable it is, how confidently it speaks, or whether it pushes back when you’re wrong? Those are different behaviors, and ideally we’d understand what inside the model contributes to each of them.

If we could identify those internal mechanisms, we could track how they change during training and test interventions. For example, could we make the model warmer without also making it more sycophantic—more likely to agree with you even when you’re mistaken?

The caveat is that finding something correlated with a personality trait doesn’t mean we’ve found a reliable control knob. We’d need to intervene and check whether the behavior actually changes across different contexts, and whether other capabilities change too. So I’d see interpretability as a way to make training more informed and measurable, rather than a guarantee that we can precisely dial in a personality.

r001.rationale: The response discusses studying internal mechanisms behind distinct behaviors, but does not state that personality differences have a structured organization in the model’s internal representation space.

r002.rationale: It proposes identifying internal mechanisms and using training interventions to shape specific traits, such as warmth without increased sycophancy, which communicates finer-grained personality control.

r003.rationale: It says interpretability could make training more informed and measurable, but does not compare its guarantees with relying solely on training data or claim stronger guarantees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interpretability could give us a way to understand what’s changing inside a model when we train it to behave a certain way. Right now, we mostly look at its responses: does it sound friendly, is it agreeable, does it push back? But similar responses could come from quite different underlying mechanisms.

If we could identify the internal representations that contribute to those behaviors, we could potentially use that information during training. For example, if you want a model to be warm without becoming sycophantic, you’d want to understand whether those traits can be separated, and whether your training is reinforcing one or both.

The caveat is that finding something correlated with a personality trait doesn’t mean you’ve found a reliable control knob. You’d need interventions to establish that it actually causes the behavior, and then check whether changing it works across different contexts. So I’d see interpretability as a way to make that training process more precise and easier to audit, rather than a guarantee that we can dial in a personality.

r001.rationale: The response says traits may be separable in internal representations, but does not state that personality differences have a structured organization in representation space.

r002.rationale: It proposes using internal representations during training to separate traits such as warmth and sycophancy, making training more precise and potentially enabling finer-grained control.

r003.rationale: It does not claim interpretability-guided training gives stronger guarantees than relying on training data; it explicitly cautions that interpretability is not a guarantee of control.
